Assertion

/uh-SUR-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Assertion means a confident statement of fact or belief, without room for doubt.

The debater opened with the bold assertion that no city had ever solved traffic by building more roads — and dared her opponents to prove otherwise.

Worked Example

At the press conference, the startup's founder made the assertion that her battery would charge any car in five minutes — a claim she delivered with complete confidence, months before independent labs had tested a single unit.

She states it as settled fact, without hedging — and without proof in hand yet. A confident claim that may or may not turn out to be backed by evidence is exactly what an assertion is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

claim: the everyday word for a statement put forward as true

declaration: stresses the open, public confidence of the statement

contention: a claim advanced in an argument, expecting pushback

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

denial: a statement that something is not true

retraction: the taking back of a statement previously made

Where it sits · how forcefully the statement is put — remark → assertion → proclamation

remark vs. assertion: A remark offers a passing thought without insisting that anyone accept it.

proclamation vs. assertion: A proclamation is announced formally and publicly, leaving even less room for doubt.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — as- (ad-)

Prefix — as- (ad-): to, toward (Latin ad-)

Root — sert-

Root — sert-: to join, bind, put in a row (Latin serere)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: act or result of (Latin -io)

Put it together

Put it together: "Assertion" literally means "a joining of oneself to" a claim — in Roman law, to assert was to bind yourself publicly to a statement, staking your own name on its truth.

Use the root in a new word: insert

Use the root in a new word: insert: She used the binding machine to insert a ribbon bookmark into each finished journal.

Word Choice

formal, academic

Assertion is a favorite of SAT reading questions: a writer's assertion is a claim stated confidently, and the passage often asks whether the evidence actually supports it. The word says nothing about being right — a bold assertion can be unproven or even false. It refers to a statement, never to a physical act; the related verb is assert.
